en: It is four minutes past nine in the evening.
On your server, the media service has just stopped answering.
OpenObserve sees it first: the error rate on Traefik is burning through its budget.
Thirty seconds later, uptime-kuma agrees: media is down.
Your usual notifications go out as always. Paeon is never in their path. It gets a copy.
Paeon records both alerts in its event log.
They are on the same host, seconds apart, so they become one incident.
No model has been called yet. This part is plain code.
Then a cheap model gets one call, with no tools.
Is this noise, something transient, a known issue, or real?
It answers: real, eighty-six percent sure.
If the model is down, or unsure, Paeon treats the incident as real. Triage fails open.
Now a strong model investigates, with tools that can only read.
It searches the Traefik logs in OpenObserve.
It inspects the container through a Docker proxy.
And it reads the last lines of the container's log.
Each tool sits behind an allow-list that you wrote.
Two minutes later, it hands in a root cause.
The media server lost its database connections during the backup, and it does not reconnect by itself.
Every claim links to the tool call behind it.
A claim with nothing behind it is marked as such.
The analysis suggests two steps.
Only one of them is in the catalog: restart the container.
The other stays a sentence, for you.
The plan goes to the executor, a separate process that checks it against its own copy of the rules.
For this alert, your policy says approve.
So the executor asks you, on your phone.
Incident three: run this fix?
The button is signed. It works once, for thirty minutes, and only for this exact plan.
You tap Go.
The executor checks that the world is still as the plan assumed.
It restarts the container, and waits until it is running and healthy.
The alerts clear, and the incident resolves.
Your phone tells you what was done, with a button to say: this was wrong.
Later, a postmortem draft is written from the same event log.
Every step you just saw is one line in an append-only log.
Models think. You say Go. Code does.
